queries.hook: I feel jealous of someone close to me. Inside, something doesn't sit right and I can't name it, and I don't know how to carry it.
queries.diagnose: Comparison and envy burn at another's success; measuring your life against theirs steals the contentment in your own.
queries.steady: Your own path, walked imperfectly, is better than another's walked well; what is yours is enough to begin with.
queries.act: Walk your own path, even imperfectly, rather than someone else's well; be grateful for what is yours and rejoice in others' good.
queries.story: A story of a seeker whose mind will not settle, facing measuring yourself against others.

hook.speaker: Bharat
hook.setting: Bharat, urged by his teacher and mother to accept the throne, explains why he cannot.
hook.sanskrit: तुम्ह तौ देहु सरल सिख सोई। जो आचरत मोर भल होई॥ जद्यपि यह समुझत हउँ नीकें। तदपि होत परितोष न जी कें ॥
hook.line: I understand your advice perfectly. My heart still isn't at peace.
hook.translation: You give me simple advice, the kind that would do me good if I followed it. Though I understand it well, my heart is not at peace.
hook.why: When head and heart disagree, go and face the person you think you wronged.

prasang.title: Bharat refuses the throne
prasang.summary: After the funeral, Vasishtha, the ministers and Kausalya all urge Bharat to rule, as his father wished. Bharat says the advice is right and his heart still isn't at peace; the crown means nothing without Ram. He decides to go to the forest, admit his fault, and trust his brother to forgive.
prasang.story_hook: Everyone agreed the throne was his, and Bharat could not bring himself to sit on it.
prasang.lesson: When head and heart disagree, go and face the person you think you wronged.

hook.for_you: You hate that you feel this way, yet understanding Bharat's advice does not bring your heart to rest.
hook.first_line: You hate that you feel this way, yet understanding Bharat's advice does not bring your heart to rest.

alternates.speaker: Bharata
alternates.setting: Grieving Kausalya accuses Bharata of plotting Ram's exile; he knew nothing of it.
alternates.sanskrit: आर्ये कस्मादजानन्तं गर्हसे मामकल्मषम्। विपुलां च मम प्रीतिं स्थितां जानासि राघवे॥
alternates.line: Why blame me, who knew nothing? You know what I feel for him.
alternates.translation: Noble lady, why do you blame me, who knew nothing and did nothing wrong? You know how deep my love for Ram is.
alternates.why: Being blamed for what you did not do hurts most from those you love; stay and make your truth known.

prasang.title: Bharata wrongly blamed
prasang.summary: Bharata turns on his mother in fury. Then Ram's grieving mother assumes he plotted it all, and her words cut him like a needle in a wound. He falls at her feet and swears his innocence until she believes him.
prasang.story_hook: He had done nothing, and the one person whose good opinion he needed was sure he had done it all.
prasang.lesson: Being blamed for what you did not do hurts most from those you love; stay and make your truth known.

alternates.speaker: Tulsidas
alternates.setting: Bharat walks toward Ram, slowed by shame, quickened by love.
alternates.sanskrit: फेरति मनहुँ मातु कृत खोरी। चलत भगति बल धीरज धोरी॥ जब समुझत रघुनाथ सुभाऊ। तब पथ परत उताइल पाऊ ॥
alternates.line: Shame slowed him. But whenever he remembered Ram's nature, his feet moved faster.
alternates.translation: It was as if his mother's wrong held him back, while the strength of devotion drove him on like a patient ox. Whenever he remembered Raghunath's nature, his feet moved faster on the path.

verse.speaker: Kakbhushundi
verse.setting: Kakbhushundi continues listing the diseases of the mind.
verse.sanskrit: ममता दादु कंडु इरषाई। हरष बिषाद गरह बहुताई॥ पर सुख देखि जरनि सोइ छई। कुष्ट दुष्टता मन कुटिलई ॥
verse.line: Envy is an itch. Burning at another's happiness is a wasting disease of the mind.
verse.translation: Possessiveness is ringworm and envy is the itch; the swings of elation and dejection are throat ailments. The burning you feel at another's happiness is consumption, and malice and a crooked mind are leprosy.
verse.why: Know your mind's diseases by name: confusion, anger, greed, envy, ego.

prasang.title: Garuda's seven questions
prasang.summary: Garuda asks seven questions: the rarest body, the greatest sorrow and joy, the nature of good and wicked people, the highest virtue and the worst wrong, and the diseases of the mind. Kakbhushundi answers: no sorrow like want, no joy like meeting good people; non-harm is highest and slander worst; delusion is the root disease, with lust, greed, anger, envy and ego as its symptoms.
prasang.lesson: Know your mind's diseases by name: confusion, anger, greed, envy, ego.

verse.try_today: Notice the burning feeling and name it as an itch of the mind.
verse.scene_line: You stand in the bathroom, and Kakbhushundi lists the diseases of the mind, naming envy as an itch.

why: The illnesses of the mind (Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand 121-122 (Gita Press))
burning at another's joy is named as an illness one suffers, which can be treated

verse.speaker: Ram
verse.setting: Ram to Bharat, who blames himself for the exile and their father's death.
verse.sanskrit: तात जायँ जियँ करहु गलानी। ईस अधीन जीव गति जानी॥ तीनि काल तिभुअन मत मोरें। पुन्यसिलोक तात तर तोरें ॥
verse.line: You torment yourself with shame for nothing. In my eyes you stand above them all.
verse.translation: Brother, you torment your heart with shame for nothing; know that a soul's course is in God's hands. In my view, all the virtuous of past, present and future, in all three worlds, stand below you.
verse.why: In family conflict, let each speak; name love plainly; lift needless shame.

matched.label: I feel ashamed of who I am

prasang.title: The family council at Chitrakoot
prasang.summary: Vasishtha asks how Ram can be brought home, noting that grieving people cannot judge well. Bharat recalls a brother who never broke his heart and let him win at games, and blames himself. Ram tells him his shame is needless, that love and hostility cannot be hidden, and asks him to say freely what he wants.
prasang.lesson: In family conflict, let each speak; name love plainly; lift needless shame.

verse.for_you: You sit with a feeling that something does not sit right after your friend's news. You do not have to carry this shame alone. The hurt you feel is not the whole truth about who you are.
verse.try_today: Notice the shame, then let it go.

why: The texts send a voice that lifts the shame: 'you torment yourself for nothing'.
the very person he believes he wronged tells him the shame is for nothing

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse.sanskrit: श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् । स्वभावनियतं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम् ॥
verse.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.
verse.why: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.
verse.misuse: Not 'stick to the role you were born into'. It's about honest fit with your own nature, not caste or family script.

prasang.title: Duties by nature, and their fruit
prasang.summary: After listing duties by varna, Krishna says one reaches perfection through one's own work done as worship, and that one's own path, though imperfect, beats another's, since every undertaking has flaws.
prasang.lesson: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.

verse.meaning: Your own duty, even when done imperfectly, is better than another's performed perfectly. Work that comes from your own nature carries no fault, and the flaws in any path are unavoidable.
verse.for_you: Your own path is the only one that can fit you. It is not wrong to feel the ache of another's success while you walk your own road. Let your own work be enough today.
verse.try_today: Notice one small task today and do it as your own.
verse.scene_line: You stand in the quiet of the bathroom, holding your own imperfect path beside her Harvard triumph.

why: settles the doubt of whether to trade one's own work for a more admired one

verse.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse.setting: 'The Common Bases of Hinduism', Lahore, November 1897.
verse.line: Learn everything that is good from others, but bring it in, and in your own way absorb it; do not become others.
verse.translation: Learn everything that is good from others, but bring it in, and in your own way absorb it; do not become others.
verse.why: Absorb the best of where you live, and grow into yourself.

prasang.title: Learn from all, imitate none (Lahore, 1897)
prasang.summary: Speaking to rival reform and orthodox groups, he looks for common ground. Religion must be realised, not repeated like a parrot. Learn everything good from others, as a seed takes in earth, air and water, but grow into your own tree and do not become others.
prasang.lesson: Absorb the best of where you live, and grow into yourself.

verse.for_you: You are allowed to feel what you feel when your friend succeeds. The good in her win can be yours without becoming her. Let your own growth stand beside her path.
verse.try_today: Notice one small way you already learn without copying anyone today.
verse.scene_line: You sit with your friend's good news and your own private ache.

why: take what is good, leave the rest

verse.speaker: Lakshman
verse.setting: After Sita is taken, Ram in fury threatens to destroy the world; Lakshman steadies him.
verse.sanskrit: एकस्य नापराधेन लोकान् हन्तुं त्वमर्हसि। ननु जानामि कस्यायं भग्नः सांग्रामिको रथः॥
verse.line: Don't punish the whole world for one person's wrong.
verse.translation: You should not destroy the worlds for the wrong done by one. Surely we can find out whose broken war chariot this is.
verse.why: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.

prasang.title: Ram's grief and Lakshman's counsel
prasang.summary: Ram returns to an empty hut. He searches, questions trees and animals, breaks down and finally rages that he will destroy the world. Lakshman calms him: don't punish the whole world for one person's crime; trouble comes to everyone and passes.
prasang.story_hook: He came back to the hut calling her name, and no one answered.
prasang.lesson: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.

verse.for_you: You can hold the ache of your friend's success and your own quiet loss. That feeling does not make you a bad person. Let your anger aim at the real cause of your hurt.
verse.try_today: Notice one small thing today that is not the reason you are hurting.
verse.scene_line: You stand in the bathroom while your friend celebrates her future, and you wonder if your own path is closing.

why: find who actually did this before acting
the innocent are kept in view

story.title: Guha nearly fights Bharat
story.story_hook: Guha saw an army on the riverbank and sank his boats.
story.summary: Seeing Bharat's army approach the Ganga, Guha assumes he is coming to kill Ram and prepares his men to die fighting. An old man reads the omens and says Bharat comes to bring Ram back. Guha agrees that fools act in haste and repent, goes to meet Bharat with gifts, and the two embrace.
story.lesson: Find out someone's intent before you prepare for war with them.
story.hook_title: Guha saw an army on the riverbank and got ready to die defending Ram
story.teaser: Guha saw an army on the riverbank and got ready to die defending Ram
story.for_you: You hate the feeling in the bathroom, and that is a sign of care. The fool acts at once and regrets it. Let the feeling sit before you do anything with it.
